span.label: an instrument: independent optical control of many sites in the brain of a freely moving animal, with the stimulated neurons recorded at the same time
span.quote: Neuronal control with high temporal precision is possible with optogenetics, yet currently available methods do not enable to control independently multiple locations in the brains of freely moving animals. Here, we describe a diode-probe system that allows real-time and location-specific control of neuronal activity at multiple sites.

span.label: how to stimulate exactly the neurons being monitored, when electrodes hear only 60 μm and every existing light source reaches far further than that
span.quote: Since such electrodes can only record and disambiguate spikes of nearby (up to 60 μm) neurons ( Buzsáki 2004 ), stimulation of continuously monitored cells requires placing the light source very close to the recording site. However, stimulation through light sources placed on the surface of the brain ( Huber et al. 2008 ) or large fibers placed in the brain parenchyma a few hundred micrometers from the recording sites ( Airan et al. 2009 ; Anikeeva et al. 2011 ; Cardin et al. 2010 ; Halassa et al. 2011 ; Han et al. 2009 ; Kravitz et al. 2010 ) inevitably activates many more unmonitored neurons than are being monitored, making the separation between direct and population-mediated effects impossible. Moreover, the high intensity used for the activation of deep neurons may generate superposition of multiple spike waveforms ( Royer et al. 2010 ) and considerable light artifacts ( Cardin et al. 2010 ; Han et al. 2009 ; Kravitz et al. 2010 ).

span.label: WHY THE LIGHT HAS TO BE WEAK AND CLOSE: electrodes can only disambiguate spikes of neurons up to 60 μm away, so stimulating from the surface or from a fiber a few hundred μm off INEVITABLY ACTIVATES MANY MORE UNMONITORED NEURONS THAN ARE BEING MONITORED, MAKING THE SEPARATION BETWEEN DIRECT AND POPULATION-MEDIATED EFFECTS IMPOSSIBLE

However, stimulation through light sources placed on the surface of the brain ( Huber et al. 2008 ) or large fibers placed in the brain parenchyma a few hundred micrometers from the recording sites ( Airan et al. 2009 ; Anikeeva et al. 2011 ; Cardin et al. 2010 ; Halassa et al. 2011 ; Han et al. 2009 ; Kravitz et al. 2010 ) inevitably activates many more unmonitored neurons than are being monitored, making the separation between direct and population-mediated effects impossible. Moreover, the high intensity used for the activation of deep neurons may generate superposition of multiple spike waveforms ( Royer et al. 2010 ) and considerable light artifacts ( Cardin et al. 2010 ; Han et al. 2009 ; Kravitz et al. 2010 ).

span.label: and strong light of ANY wavelength carries energy dissipated as HEAT, which has a MIXED DE-/HYPERPOLARIZING effect - a confound that does not depend on the opsin at all
span.quote: Second, strong light of any wavelength carries considerable energy that is dissipated in the form of heat as photons are scattered and absorbed in brain tissue. Local heating has a mixed de-/hyperpolarizing effect on neuronal activity ( Shen and Schwartzkroin 1988 ; Thompson et al. 1985 ), which may confound and/or limit the effect of optogenetic manipulations. Third, high-intensity light may generate photoelectrical artifacts manifested as LFP deflections ( Cardin et al. 2010 ; Han et al. 2009 ; Kravitz et al. 2010 ) and cause synchronous activation of nearby neurons ( Royer et al. 2010 ), limiting the interpretability of induced LFP patterns and the use of spike-sorting techniques.

span.label: THE SAME LIGHT, THE OPPOSITE SIGN, DECIDED BY THE PROMOTER: identical parameters in CA1 give robust spiking of pyramidal cells in CaMKII::ChR2 mice, and in PV::ChR2 mice spiking of interneurons FOLLOWED BY SILENCING of the nearby pyramidal cells
span.quote: When placed in the CA1 region of CaMKII::ChR2 mice, blue light stimulation (50 ms, ∼0.9 mW/mm 2 at the shank center) resulted in robust spiking of putative pyramidal cells but not of interneurons ( Fig. 5 E , left ). In contrast, blue light stimulation with identical parameters in the CA1 of PV::ChR2 mice resulted in robust spiking of interneurons followed by silencing of nearby pyramidal cells ( Fig. 5 E , right ). Thus diode probes enable spatiotemporal control of specific cell types in various species.

span.label: A 25% CHANGE IN DOSE FLIPS THE OUTCOME: 70% of the 0.35 mW/mm 2 blue pulses overcame the red-light hyperpolarization but ONLY 10% of the 0.28 mW/mm 2 pulses did - the same two opsins, the same cells, and a sharp threshold between activation and silencing
span.quote: Notably, the ability of ChR2-induced depolarization to overcome the halo-induced hyperpolarization depended sharply on blue light intensity: 70% of the 0.35 mW/mm 2 blue-light pulses but only 10% of 0.28 mW/mm 2 pulses were efficient (χ 2 -test, P < 0.01). Thus diode probes enable activation and silencing of the same neurons in freely behaving animals.

span.label: a statistical definition rescued by the data's own shape: the definition of light-modulated spiking WAS STATISTICAL, but the modulation indices exhibited a BIMODAL distribution, 0.045 against 0.76
span.quote: Although the definition of light-modulated spiking was statistical, light modulation indices (difference between firing rates during photostimulation and baseline divided by the sum) exhibited a bimodal distribution (medians for nonresponsive/light-modulated units, 0.045/0.76; U test, P < 0.001; Fig. 4 B , middle ).

span.label: THE UNIT IS DEFINED BY THREE NUMBERED GATES BEFORE ANY RESULT IS COMPUTED: peak-to-peak amplitude above 50 microvolts, L ratio below 0.05, and a clear refractory period - and then a fourth for the statistics, at least 100 spikes above 0.01 spikes/s
span.quote: Units were required to fulfill the following criteria: 1 ) amplitude: peak-to-peak amplitude >50 μV; 2 ) morphological isolation: L ratio ( Schmitzer-Torbert et al. 2005 ) below 0.05; and 3 ) temporal isolation: interspike-interval histogram with a clear refractory period (count in the 1st 2 ms below 0.2 of the expected count given the counts in the 1st 20 ms; Fee et al. 1996 ). A total of 535 hippocampal and 98 neocortical units conformed to these criteria. To be included in statistical analyses ( Figs. 4 – 6 ), units were required to fire at least 100 spikes at a baseline rate >0.01 spikes/s; this yielded a data set of 135/72 hippocampal units (rat/mouse) and 39 neocortical units (rat).

span.label: an idealisation declared inside a figure legend: the estimate ASSUMES neuronal density of 20,000 cells/mm 3 and IGNORES SHADOWING by the probe shank

Latencies were similar for units recorded in different regions of the hippocampus (CA1, dentate gyrus, and CA3; median latencies: 6/6.5/5 ms; Kruskal-Wallis test, P = 0.61; Fig. 5 A , inset ). Finally, the temporal precision of light-evoked spiking, quantified by the across-trial standard deviation of the centers-of-mass, was in the millisecond range (median, 2 ms; Fig. 5 A , right ), indicating that weak blue light could yield precise temporal control of concurrently recorded units.

span.quote: Examining the circuit and behavioral impact of spatiotemporally sequenced activity at different timescales could address the debate on rate vs. temporal coding ( Shadlen and Newsome 1998 ).

span.label: and the synthetic pattern is taken up by the native one: units driven by nonperiodic photostimuli exhibited PHASE PRECESSION, indicating that NATIVE NETWORK DYNAMICS CAN INCORPORATE SYNTHETIC PATTERNS OF ACTIVITY
span.quote: Moreover, these units exhibited phase precession ( O'Keefe and Recce 1993 ; slopes of circular-linear fit: 0.4 and 1.2°/cm; permutation test: P < 0.01 and P < 0.05; Fig. 8 C , bottom ), indicating that native network dynamics can incorporate synthetic patterns of activity. Thus spatially localized photostimulation can be used to probe the mechanisms of naturally generated network activity.
